source.title_on_document: Effects of Personalized Generative AI on Student Creativity: Evidence from Creative Performance, Self-efficacy, and Attention Allocation

supplement.holds: The chapter refers to no supplement or online appendix. All reported statistics are in the main text (Sect. 4.1, Fig. 4, Tables 1 and 2).

paper_design_summary: Sixty-two university students (32 undergraduates, 30 graduate students) each did two Product Improvement Tasks in a laboratory, one with standard ChatGPT-4 and one with a personalized GPT-4 tutor (Mr. Ranedeer), with the order counterbalanced across two halves of 31. Two trained raters blind to condition scored each participant's solutions for quality, elaboration, and originality on 1-5 scales. The paper also measures creative self-efficacy by questionnaire and attention allocation by eye tracking, and compares conditions with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

studies.label: Within-subject laboratory experiment: personalized GAI (Mr. Ranedeer) vs standard GAI (ChatGPT-4) on the Product Improvement Task

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the two GAI conditions (standard ChatGPT-4 first then Mr. Ranedeer, or the reverse). Every participant used both tools.
assignment.quote: A counterbalanced design was used: half completed the first task with ChatGPT-4 and the second with Mr. Ranedeer, while the other half followed the reverse order.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 381), Sect. 3.3 Procedure; Fig. 2

arms.name: Personalized GAI (Mr. Ranedeer)
arms.description: GPT-4-powered tutor customized on OpenAI's Explore GPTs platform; three stages: personalization of learning preferences and plan design, Socratic heuristic questioning, solution elaboration with goal-aligned feedback and strategic prompts.

arms.name: Standard GAI (ChatGPT-4)
arms.description: ChatGPT-4 giving generic feedback in two stages: broad suggestions in response to queries, then solution generation on request.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The paper states 62 participants (31 per order group in Fig. 2) and does not restate N in the results; it does not say the order was randomly assigned, so no count is coded as randomized.
participants.who: 32 undergraduates and 30 graduate students, 33.9% male, ages 18-27 (M = 22.6, SD = 2.5), from social sciences, life sciences, and technical disciplines; almost all had prior GAI experience; compensated.
participants.country: Not stated for participants; all author affiliations are in China (Zhejiang, Shanghai).
participants.quote: Sixty-two students (32 undergraduates and 30 graduate students; 33.9% male) participated in the study.
participants.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 379), Sect. 3.1 Participants; Fig. 2 on PDF p. 6 (N = 31 per order group)

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4 (standard) and Mr. Ranedeer, a custom GPT built on OpenAI GPT-4 via Explore GPTs (personalized)
ai_tool.how_used: Participants did the task through the OpenAI web interface, chatting with the assigned GAI in a split screen next to a workspace where they typed their solutions. The personalized tutor asked about preferences, used Socratic questioning, and then gave goal-aligned feedback and idea-refinement prompts; ChatGPT-4 gave broad suggestions and generated solutions on request.

task.description: Product Improvement Task (Torrance, 1966): propose three solutions as original and useful as possible to improve a common product (e.g., a stuffed bunny and a portable coffee machine), one product per task.
task.duration: About 17 min (SD = 7) in the standard condition and 20 min (SD = 6) in the personalized condition; 5-minute break between tasks.

outcomes.name: Creative performance: quality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two trained raters blind to condition rated solutions on a 1-5 Likert scale (quality = extent the solution addresses the task objective); solutions presented in randomized order; inter-rater reliability Cronbach's alpha = 0.88; final score = average of the two raters. Rater expertise not described beyond 'trained'.

contrasts.reported: Personalized M = 3.50, SD = 1.00 vs standard M = 3.08, SD = 1.12; Wilcoxon signed-rank p = .001; r = .42 (N = 62 within-subject; Z not reported)
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 383), Sect. 4.1; Fig. 4A on PDF p. 9

outcomes.name: Creative performance: elaboration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same two blinded trained raters, 1-5 Likert scale (elaboration = amount of detail provided); Cronbach's alpha = 0.90; average of the two raters.

contrasts.reported: Personalized M = 3.58, SD = 1.17 vs standard M = 2.48, SD = 1.04; Wilcoxon signed-rank p < .001; r = .62 (N = 62 within-subject; Z not reported)
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 383), Sect. 4.1; Fig. 4A on PDF p. 9

outcomes.name: Creative performance: originality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same two blinded trained raters, 1-5 Likert scale (originality = novelty of the idea); Cronbach's alpha = 0.86; average of the two raters.

contrasts.reported: Personalized M = 2.92, SD = 1.15 vs standard M = 3.13, SD = 1.27; Wilcoxon signed-rank p = .098; r = .18 (N = 62 within-subject; Z not reported)
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 383), Sect. 4.1; Fig. 4A on PDF p. 9

eligibility.reason: Within-person comparison of two AI configurations (personalized GPT-4 tutor vs standard ChatGPT-4) with 62 students and blinded human ratings of the solutions. The order was counterbalanced (half and half, 31 per group), but the paper never says the order was randomly assigned, so criterion 1 is unclear. There is no no-AI arm; the contrast is ai_design. 62 people is above 50.

one_line_finding: With the personalized GPT-4 tutor, students' product-improvement solutions were rated higher than with standard ChatGPT-4 on quality (3.50 vs 3.08, p = .001, r = .42) and elaboration (3.58 vs 2.48, p < .001, r = .62), but not on originality (2.92 vs 3.13, p = .098) (PDF p. 8, Sect. 4.1).
open_questions: Was the order of conditions randomly assigned? The paper says only 'counterbalanced design' with half in each order (PDF p. 6).

Which product went with which task position, and was product counterbalanced against condition? The paper names two products ('e.g., a stuffed bunny and a portable coffee machine') but does not say how products were paired with conditions or order.
Is the unit of the Wilcoxon tests the participant's mean over three solutions? The paper implies paired participant-level data but does not say how the three solutions were aggregated.

Possible overlap: the retrieval log notes a separate Chen and Huang paper (AJET 2026, personalised GenAI feedback and creative problem-solving, N = 62). This chapter does not mention it, so no overlap is recorded here; worth checking whether the participants are the same.
notes: Non-output outcomes are not listed as outcomes: creative self-efficacy (self-report, 7-point scale; personalized M = 5.24, SD = 0.99 vs standard M = 4.89, SD = 1.19; p = .033; r = .26; PDF p. 8) and eye-tracking measures (Table 1, PDF p. 9: mean fixation duration in AOI 1, p = .465; AOI 3, p = .756; number of transitions 219.37 vs 178.66, Z = -2.39, p = .017, r = 0.30). Table 2 (PDF p. 10) reports within-condition correlations among outcomes. Fig. 4 error bars are standard deviations. The scored output was produced with AI available in both conditions. Raters coded as human_raters because the paper calls them 'two trained raters' without describing domain expertise.
